articles.title: Family legacy helps explain how heirs decide to donate inherited possessions
articles.dek: by Phil Ciciora, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
paragraphs: by Phil Ciciora, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

There's a good reason why that fine china set or crystal stemware collection inherited from grandma sits in a box gathering dust in the basement. According to new research co-written by a University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign marketing expert, consumers don't simply donate family heirlooms and move on from them when they no longer spark joy. Instead, they remain concerned with how those heritage goods will be passed on to new owners and whether their legacy will continue.

As the households of the baby boom generation downsize, their adult children continue to face difficult decisions about what to do with the sometimes unwanted leftover goods bequeathed to them. A new paper indicates that descendants who inherit meaningful possessions often opt to keep heritage goods together as a set rather than breaking them up and giving them away piecemeal, said Ravi Mehta, the Walter H. Stellner Professor of Marketing at Illinois.

"While previous research has focused on why people hold on to meaningful possessions, this research examines what happens when letting go of those possessions becomes necessary," said Mehta, also the associate dean of graduate programs and a professor of business administration at Gies College of Business.
The study is published in the Journal of the Association for Consumer Research .

Across a qualitative pilot study and four experiments, the researchers found that heirs thought keeping items together when giving them away helped preserve the family history and legacy embedded in the heritage goods. However, when goods such as dinnerware or hardcover books were viewed as independent pieces rather than a unified whole, heirs became more willing to distribute them across multiple charities if doing so increased the likelihood that the items would continue to be used.

"We found that people prefer to maintain the systemic integrity and sanctity of the product, even when they are giving it away for free," Mehta said. "In other words, if it's a dish set, they chose to keep all the dishes together and donate the entire set rather than breaking it apart and spreading it out over many different charities."
The findings revealed that consumers remain concerned about the fate of heritage goods long after their ownership of them ends, Mehta said.

"More broadly, the research highlights that facilitating the circulation of heritage goods may require addressing not only practical concerns such as who gets what but also the psychological needs of heirs—specifically, their desire to see their family history and legacy continue in some sort of useful manner in the future," he said.
The research has implications for charities, donation platforms and organizations involved in reuse and resale, the researchers said.

"For many families right now with aging parents and relatives, this is a very relevant issue," Mehta said. "The results suggest that heirs may be more willing to donate heritage goods when they believe the goods' legacy will be preserved—either by keeping items together or by ensuring that individual pieces continue to be appropriately used."

articles.title: Paying for the past: Norway's finder's fees favor gold's weight over what it tells us
articles.dek: Ten years ago, in 2016, a metal detectorist came upon a hoard of gold.
paragraphs: Ten years ago, in 2016, a metal detectorist came upon a hoard of gold. It had been buried in the dirt for around 1,800 years and consisted of around 396 grams (14 ounces) of gold rings. The detectorist handed in his finds to a museum and received the largest finder's fee ever paid out in Norwegian history. He had been rewarded for the gold weight, not its rarity.
Meanwhile, around two years earlier, another find, considerably less heavy but far rarer, had earned a comparatively higher reward relative to its weight. Its finder was paid for its uniqueness.

A new study published in Public Archaeology took a closer look at how Norway's reward system ranks its golden objects and found that it often values an object's weight and rarity over what it can tell us about history.

Common finds are often deemed "mass material" and are therefore considered less valuable than a rare find, said study author Irmelin Axelsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Oslo, even though mass material "can tell us something about groups and patterns, which singular artifacts cannot, because they're precisely that, outliers."

If you live in Norway and stumble upon a gold or silver object older than A. D. 1537, that object is considered state property and needs to be handed in, the study reported. As a reward for finding the archaeological artifact, you're paid the metal's current value plus 10%.

But two cases show the law isn't quite so straightforward. In 2016, the Skaun hoard, made up of 17 golden rings, was discovered and took the media by storm. Archaeologists at NTNU University Museum were quoted as describing it as a "fantastic" and "truly unique" find. Yet a few months later, they changed their minds, deeming it a common find of so-called "payment gold."

The museum suggested that the Skaun hoard's finder should be paid 155,000 Norwegian kroner, about €17,000. The reward was based on the weight of the find. The sum broke records, and yet the detectorist called it unusual, recalling a similar find made a few years earlier that had weighed far less and yet been valued more per gram of gold.
Tornes consisted of only five gold objects weighing roughly 19 grams (0. 67 ounces). And yet the finder's fee amounted to 73,000 kroner. It was rewarded for its rarity.

Axelsen explained the apparent contradiction, saying that archaeologists had already found "so many pieces of payment gold that the potential for new knowledge based on that particular find was seen as low, thus making its perceived cultural-historical value less than that of a rare find."
Wanting to get a better idea of how Norway values its golden finds, Axelsen and her co-author Mats Skare took a closer look at 191 golden objects housed in Norwegian museums.

They ranked each piece by how confidently they could date it. They found that only 105 of the objects could be dated, and nearly half of those could not be pinned down to within a window of around 350 years or older.

The remainder constituted golden scraps and glimmering fragments, objects that, historically speaking, could say next to nothing. The finds highlight how, in many cases, a lump of gold weighing 3–5 grams (0. 11–0. 18 ounces) could earn more than a datable and recognizable piece of cultural-historical value.

Inconsistencies in how gold is valued are put into even starker contrast when one considers that the price of gold is ever fluctuating and payments often take a long time to be made. The Skaun hoard would be worth three times more today than in 2021, the study reported.

The authors write that finders, faced with fluctuating gold prices and the prospect of inconsistent payouts, may feel incentivized to keep, sell, or even melt down gold objects, the very thing the finder's fee is meant to prevent.

articles.title: Q&A: What's innovative about canned food?
articles.dek: To most consumers, canned food is an everyday convenience, but to John Coupland, professor of food science at Penn State, each can represents more than two centuries of…
paragraphs: To most consumers, canned food is an everyday convenience, but to John Coupland, professor of food science at Penn State, each can represents more than two centuries of invention, experimentation and problem-solving.

In his new book, "Containing Nature: The Ongoing Invention of Canned Food," Coupland traces the evolution of canned food from its origins in late 18th-century France through the scientific breakthroughs, manufacturing advances and public health innovations that transformed the modern food system.

In this Q&A, Coupland discussed the hidden history of cans, the unexpected connections between military rations and grocery store staples and why the most familiar items still have the power to inspire wonder.

Coupland: The idea has been simmering for a long time. When I interviewed for my faculty position at Penn State decades ago, part of the process included visiting a local canned food factory. I walked in as a young scientist and realized I was surrounded by people with tremendous expertise that was very different from my own. These were people who had spent generations figuring out how to turn vegetables into a successful business. That experience stuck with me.

Years later, after serving as president of the Institute of Food Technologists and teaching Penn State's large general education course "Food Facts and Fads" about food and culture, I became increasingly interested in how people develop expertise and how technologies evolve. Canning turned out to be the perfect lens.

Coupland: The inventor of canning, Nicolas Appert, was a leader in the French Revolution. He even escorted the king to the guillotine. There is a myth that he was somehow paid to develop military rations by Napoleon, but, in fact, his workshop was destroyed twice during the Napoleonic Wars.

It's interesting that Appert had no scientific training and made his discoveries by trial and error while making products for sale in his high-end grocery store in Paris. Ironically, the first scientists who tried to explain canning were completely wrong, not because they lacked intelligence, but because they were working with the knowledge available at the time.
Later advances in bacteriology and food science helped explain why foods spoil and how to prevent it. Science is a process of building knowledge, revising ideas and responding to new questions.

Coupland: The first London canners were successful because the British wanted to send ships to explore the Arctic. These missions took several years, and so the navy would pay a premium for preserved foods to keep the sailors alive through the long, cold winters when the ships were trapped in ice.

Before reliable preservation, long voyages were constrained by which foods could survive the journey. Canned foods made it possible to travel farther and remain at sea longer. They helped support military expeditions, exploration and global trade. In many cases, advances in preservation expanded what people believed was possible because they removed one of the biggest logistical challenges: feeding people safely over time.

One thing that stood out throughout writing the book is how often necessity drives innovation. Many developments in food preservation emerged from the needs of the military or explorers. Even modern retort pouches, like baby food packets, can trace their roots to solving practical problems for soldiers.

Coupland: Food safety concerns drove some of the most important innovations in the history of canning. Canners had developed new methods for sterilizing cans using pressure cookers, but they didn't understand the conditions that worked best, and there were some tragic cases of botulism.

The need for a scientific understanding of botulism and other hazards led to an intense research effort in the 1920s, resulting in improvements in standards and food safety. It's a good example of how science can support technology in response to a pressing need, but it also illustrates that technological achievement often comes before scientific understanding.

articles.title: Parental benefit encouraged people to have children in Estonia, but fathers mainly applied for financial reasons
articles.dek: A generous parental leave reform was introduced in Estonia in 2004. This increased the likelihood of a second or third child being born into the family and also shortened the…
paragraphs: A generous parental leave reform was introduced in Estonia in 2004. This increased the likelihood of a second or third child being born into the family and also shortened the interval between births, according to Sanan Abdullayev's doctoral thesis , defended at Tallinn University. At the same time, taking shared parental leave did not necessarily mean that the father took time off work and assumed primary responsibility for the children while receiving the benefit.

Prior to the 2004 parental leave reform, a child's caregiver could take a long period of parental leave, but childcare allowances were paid at the same low rates to everyone. The reform shortened the period over which the benefit is paid, but linked the amount of the benefit to the parent's previous income. Thus, the benefit generally began to compensate for the previous earnings of the parent staying at home with the child.
Parents who had their next child within 30 months of the birth of their previous child were able to retain the rate of benefit they had been receiving prior to the birth of their previous child.

Abdullayev, a recent Ph. D. graduate from the School of Governance, Law and Society, used data from Estonian national registers to investigate how the 2004 reform affected families. Abdullayev's doctoral thesis is the first study to use composite models to analyze the impact of family policy measures.
As a result, it is now possible for the first time to distinguish whether family policy primarily influenced the likelihood of having a subsequent child or the interval between births.

Based on an analysis of data on the entire permanent population of childbearing age in Estonia, the study found that the reform increased the likelihood of having a second and third child and also shortened the interval between births. The impact was strongest among mothers with a higher education qualification, for whom the benefit compensated for the majority of their previous income.

At the same time, the likelihood of having another child also increased among mothers with lower levels of education and income. As a result of the reform, parents who had previously been unemployed began to receive benefits close to the minimum wage. Consequently, the reform provided some parents with additional household income.

The doctoral thesis also examined the use of shared parental leave . Parents' income was the most important factor in predicting which parent would make use of the benefit. The more a father earned compared to the child's mother, the more likely he was to claim the parental benefit. However, this did not necessarily mean that the father stayed home instead of going to work.

Around 70% of fathers who received the parental benefit were working at least part time during their leave in order to boost their family's total income. This is possible because Estonia's family policy allows parents to receive parental benefits while continuing to work.

Consequently, in the Estonian context, a father receiving the parental benefit cannot be interpreted as him taking primary responsibility for childcare, but rather as a financial decision aimed at improving the family's financial situation.

One finding of the doctoral thesis was that a father's use of paternity leave was associated with a higher probability of a third child being born into the family, and within a shorter time frame. The link was particularly clear in families where the mother returned to paid work while the father received paternity benefits.

The doctoral thesis shows that the Estonian parental benefit has fulfilled one of its main objectives: A generous income-related allowance paid over a sufficiently long period may increase the likelihood of having another child.

At the same time, the study shows that, when assessing the impact of family policy, one should look not only at which parent receives the benefit, but also at how the burden of childcare is actually shared between the parents.

Estonia’s 2004 income-linked parental benefit reform increased the likelihood of second and third births and shortened birth intervals, especially among highly educated mothers. Fathers’ claims mainly reflected financial incentives; about 70% continued working at least part time, so benefit receipt did not reliably indicate primary childcare responsibility.

articles.title: Scientists Develop a Remarkable New Coating for the Powerhouses of Our Cells
articles.dek: Scientists have given the tiny powerhouses of our cells a remarkable high-tech makeover that preserves their energy production and could pave the way for future treatments.
paragraphs: Scientists have given the tiny powerhouses of our cells a remarkable high-tech makeover that preserves their energy production and could pave the way for future treatments.

Scientists have developed a way to coat mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing energy inside cells, with advanced materials without interfering with their ability to function. The breakthrough could eventually help researchers develop new approaches to treating diseases caused by malfunctioning mitochondria.

The discovery comes from a collaboration between IRCCS Fondazione Istituto Neurologico Carlo Besta (FINCB) and Politecnico di Milano. The work was conducted through the BraiNs joint laboratory and published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS) .

The project combines the expertise of two research teams. One is led by Dr. Valeria Tiranti (FINCB), who works in the Medical Genetics and Neurogenetics Complex Unit (SC) and heads the Fondazione Mariani Center for Pediatric Mitochondrial Diseases. The other is led by Professor Pierangelo Metrangolo (Politecnico di Milano), whose team specializes in chemistry and materials engineering.

Often described as the powerhouses of cells, mitochondria generate the energy needed to keep essential cellular processes running. When they malfunction, they can contribute to a range of medical conditions, including rare mitochondrial diseases.

These disorders are particularly harmful to tissues that require large amounts of energy, such as the brain and muscles. Treatment options remain limited, making new strategies for working with mitochondria especially valuable.

The researchers focused on a class of advanced materials known as Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOF). These materials can be customized for different purposes by adjusting their properties. Their scientific importance was recognized with the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi.

Applying these materials to mitochondria presents a considerable challenge because the cellular structures are extremely delicate. Even small changes to their surroundings could potentially interfere with their essential functions.
To overcome this difficulty, the researchers developed a technique that allows them to apply very small quantities of the materials directly to the mitochondrial surface.

Most importantly, the mitochondria continued producing energy after receiving the coating. This demonstrates that their surfaces can be modified with these materials without compromising their energy generating function.

The ability to customize the coating could make the technique useful for a variety of future applications. By changing the material’s properties, researchers may eventually be able to create coatings designed to carry out specific tasks.

“The possibility of modifying the coating now opens up new research prospects: in the future, it will be possible to develop MOF with different characteristics depending on the objective, creating coatings capable of performing specific functions,” observes Prof. Metrangolo.

One potential application involves mitochondrial transplantation, an experimental strategy that seeks to introduce healthy mitochondria into cells whose existing mitochondria are not functioning properly.
“A specifically designed coating could, in the future, facilitate this transfer and the interaction between mitochondria and cells,” emphasizes Dr. Tiranti.

articles.title: Scientists discover dangerous water oscillations between Lake Varna and Black Sea
articles.dek: For years, pilots have observed strong and unusual currents in the 2. 4-kilometer-long (1. 5-mile-long), 300-meter-wide (984-foot-wide) canal connecting Lake Varna with the…
paragraphs: For years, pilots have observed strong and unusual currents in the 2. 4-kilometer-long (1. 5-mile-long), 300-meter-wide (984-foot-wide) canal connecting Lake Varna with the Black Sea. Maarja Kruusmaa, an academician and professor at Tallinn University of Technology, and researcher Laura Piho, working with the Port of Varna, undertook detailed measurements to determine the causes of the phenomenon.

"For this, we used Hydromast measuring stations developed at Tallinn University of Technology's Center for Biorobotics. Three of the stations recorded the speed and direction of water movement as well as water levels at one-minute intervals," Piho explained.

Jüri Elken, professor emeritus of oceanography, joined them to help explain the unusual water movements. The broader aim of the Estonian researchers' measurements is to gain a better understanding of flow dynamics in canals. Such knowledge can also help other regions facing similar problems respond effectively, including by improving vessel navigation, forecasting the development of strong currents and providing rapid warnings about changing currents.

The measurements confirmed that, in addition to normal moderate water movement, strong oscillations with periods of several dozen minutes can occur in the canal connecting Lake Varna, on the western coast of the Black Sea, to the sea.

"Oscillations with periods of 37 and 19 minutes were particularly pronounced," Elken emphasized. According to the Estonian researchers, these are linked to resonance in the canal–Lake Varna system, which can significantly amplify water movement under certain atmospheric conditions.

Two exceptionally strong events were recorded during the study. In the first, water oscillations began abruptly and lasted for a couple of cycles. They were caused by a meteorological tsunami, which can occur when a weather front moves over shallow coastal waters at what is known as resonance speed.
According to the researchers, the second significant event occurred more than five hours after a storm when offshore winds reached 20 meters per second (45 miles per hour).

Over a 10-minute period, the largest changes in current velocity reached 0. 8 meters per second (1. 8 miles per hour), while water levels changed by as much as 0. 8 meters (2. 6 feet). The authors noted that fluctuations this strong make passage through the canal highly dangerous for vessels, disrupt port operations and make coastal management more difficult overall.

The study's results provide an opportunity to advance knowledge of water movement patterns, which could support port management and navigational safety as well as contribute to environmental impact assessments.

The researchers therefore say it is important to study events in which strong currents and resonant sea-level fluctuations lasting less than an hour occur in marine bays and in channels connecting them with upstream lakes and rivers.

Elken, Piho and Kruusmaa emphasized that while their study also proposes specific steps for developing coastal monitoring and forecasting systems, the scientific paper primarily demonstrates how high-temporal-resolution measurements combined with mathematical modeling can help identify and predict hazardous water oscillations that might otherwise go undetected.

Measurements in the canal linking Lake Varna to the Black Sea identified resonant oscillations with periods of 37 and 19 minutes. Extreme events involved current velocity changes of up to 0. 8 m/s and water-level changes of up to 0. 8 m within 10 minutes, creating navigation hazards. High-resolution monitoring and modeling can help detect and predict these oscillations.

articles.title: Sapphire-grown semiconductor film sets bandgap record
articles.dek: Semiconductors with wider bandgaps could pave the way for smaller, more efficient electronics that can handle far higher voltages, but the wider this gap becomes, the harder…
paragraphs: Semiconductors with wider bandgaps could pave the way for smaller, more efficient electronics that can handle far higher voltages, but the wider this gap becomes, the harder it is to control how well a material conducts electricity. Now, a team led by Darrell Schlom at Cornell University has shown that adding silicon to thin films of aluminum gallium oxide can keep this control intact at bandgaps wider than any semiconductor before it. Their research has been published in Nature .

In a semiconductor, electrons occupy two distinct ranges of energy. In the lower "valence band," they are bound tightly to their atoms and can't carry a current. If they gain enough energy, however, they can jump into the higher "conduction band," where they move freely.

A semiconductor's bandgap describes the energy required for an electron to make this leap and allows semiconductors to be switched between insulating and conducting states. Since wider bandgaps let materials withstand stronger electric fields, wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride and silicon carbide are already used in everything from fast phone chargers to electric vehicles.

Aluminum gallium oxide is an especially promising material. By adjusting its ratio of aluminum to gallium, its bandgap can be tuned anywhere from 5. 4 to 8. 6 electronvolts (eV), the widest range of any known semiconductor. But as the aluminum content rises, it becomes far harder to supply the material with free electrons. Until now, aluminum-rich films have conducted electricity several orders of magnitude more poorly than gallium-rich ones, which has made them impractical for electronics.

Schlom's team tackled this challenge through a careful fabrication approach involving a sapphire substrate. To grow the oxide films, they applied a technique called molecular-beam epitaxy, which builds up a material one atomic layer at a time.

As each film grew on top of the sapphire, they added small amounts of silicon, whose atoms donate spare electrons to the material. Finally, they measured the films' bandgaps and electrical properties and tested how the films behaved inside two key electronic components: a diode and a transistor.

The silicon-doped films conducted electricity at bandgaps of more than 7 eV, beating the previous record held by cubic boron nitride. Above 6 eV, a range the team calls "colossal bandgap," the films conducted electricity at room temperature over 100 million times better than any previous report. Both the diode and the transistor worked successfully with these colossal-bandgap materials.

The approach could also make next-generation semiconductors far more practical to produce. Compared with other ultra-wide-bandgap materials like diamond and cubic boron nitride, sapphire is abundant, cheap and already manufactured at high quality at a massive scale.

Based on their success, Schlom's team now hopes that their films could pave the way for a new generation of power electronics that waste far less energy as heat when converting and controlling electricity.

articles.title: A Single Gene Could Hold the Key to Taming One of the Deadliest Cancers
articles.dek: Blocking one gene’s activity shifted aggressive pancreatic cancer cells into a less aggressive form in experiments, pointing to a possible way to disrupt tumor evolution.
paragraphs: Blocking one gene’s activity shifted aggressive pancreatic cancer cells into a less aggressive form in experiments, pointing to a possible way to disrupt tumor evolution.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma kills nearly 85 percent of people within five years of diagnosis. Part of the challenge is that its cancer cells can change, shifting between less aggressive and more aggressive forms in ways that earlier studies could not explain.

A study led by researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center now shows how genetic reshaping within individual tumors enables those transitions. Published in Nature Genetics , the findings suggest that ongoing changes to cancer cells’ DNA help fuel both resistance to treatment and metastasis, the spread of cancer to other parts of the body.

More than half a dozen genes have been implicated in this complex disease. Earlier research generally measured increases and decreases in gene activity across groups of cells analyzed together, separating pancreatic cancer cells into two broad subtypes: classical, which is less aggressive, and basal, which is more aggressive. Those bulk measurements could not explain how cells switched between the two.

To examine the differences among individual cells, the researchers used transcriptomics, which measures gene activity. They analyzed 443,451 single cells from 62 tumors in 56 men and women with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Six patients provided tumor samples both before and after chemotherapy, allowing the team to examine changes across treatment.

“Our study provides the most granular view to date of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, revealing how ongoing genetic reshaping drives tumor evolution over the course of disease,” said study lead investigator Despoina Kalfakakou, PhD, a postdoctoral research fellow at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and Perlmutter Cancer Center.

Within the tumors, the team identified clones, groups of cells with similar genetic makeup. Individual tumors contained between two and 11 clones on average, with mixtures of basal and classical cells. These groups behaved differently as they evolved, with some developing resistance to therapy and others acquiring the ability to spread rapidly.

“Our research also suggests that single-cell clonal analysis offers a better approach to understanding complex cancers, like pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, as it develops over time, by mapping how tumors evolve and adapt at each stage of disease progression,” said study co-senior investigator Aristotelis Tsirigos, PhD, a professor in the Departments of Medicine and Pathology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a member of Perlmutter Cancer Center.

Using patterns of gene activity to trace the clones’ genetic origins, the researchers linked variations in DNA copy number to the mix of cells making up each tumor. This helped them identify which genes were most active at different stages of disease progression. Among the changes associated with tumor evolution was increased activity of a gene called MYC in aggressive tumor cell populations.

In further experiments with basal pancreatic tumor cells, blocking MYC activity returned the cells to the less aggressive classical form. It also exposed them to more immune cells, potentially making them more vulnerable to immune attack. “These findings suggest that targeting the mechanisms underlying tumor evolution, including MYC, may help restrain the cancer’s rapid progression,” Kalfakakou said.

Other differences among clones offered clues to why this cancer resists immunotherapy. In some clones, the TIGIT gene was more active, producing proteins that help cancer evade immune detection. In those same cells, activity of the PD1 gene was suppressed, which may help explain why some immunotherapies targeting PD1 are rarely effective against the disease.

“More broadly, our study results highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, genetic plasticity, and interactions with the tumor’s microenvironment in shaping human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma biology,” said Dr. Tsirigos, who also serves as co-director of the Division of Precision Medicine and director of NYU Langone’s Applied Bioinformatics Laboratories.

Clinical trials of MYC inhibitors or TIGIT inhibitors for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and other cancers are underway, Tsirigos said. He added that the findings should encourage larger investigations into the different states cancer cells can occupy and how treatments might target them.

articles.title: Scientists Discover That One Common Protein Source Makes Gut Inflammation Much Worse
articles.dek: A diet’s protein source may influence how severely the gut becomes inflamed, with mouse experiments offering clues for more tailored dietary guidance for people with…
paragraphs: A diet’s protein source may influence how severely the gut becomes inflamed, with mouse experiments offering clues for more tailored dietary guidance for people with inflammatory bowel disease.

The protein on your plate may do more than build muscle. Growing evidence suggests that where dietary protein comes from could influence inflammation in the gut, raising important questions about how food choices might affect people living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

IBD includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, two chronic conditions in which abnormal immune responses contribute to ongoing inflammation in the digestive tract. Symptoms can include persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, fatigue, and intestinal bleeding, often alternating between periods of remission and unpredictable flare-ups. Although genetics, immune function, and gut microbes all play important roles, researchers are still working to understand how diet influences the disease.

IBD has also become increasingly common in the United States and worldwide over recent decades, alongside shifts in dietary habits that include greater consumption of animal protein. Despite these trends, scientists have yet to establish clear, evidence-based recommendations about which protein sources might be most beneficial for people with IBD.

As the authors explain, “Although diet is believed to be an important contributor to the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel diseases, there are few evidence-based dietary recommendations for patients to lessen disease severity.”

A new study in Cellular and Molecular Gastroenterology explored whether the source of dietary protein could change the severity of intestinal inflammation. Researchers compared diets containing beef, egg, dairy, soy, or pea protein across multiple mouse models of IBD.

Mice fed beef protein consistently developed the most severe intestinal inflammation, while those consuming pea protein experienced the least inflammation and only mild symptoms. The pattern remained consistent across the different models and in both male and female mice.
“Mice fed a beef protein diet exhibited the most severe colitis, whereas mice fed pea protein developed mild inflammation,” the authors say.
Importantly, beef protein alone did not cause overt intestinal inflammation in mice without a colitis trigger, suggesting that its effects depend on other factors involved in the disease.

The findings point to interactions between gut microbes, the intestinal barrier, and bile acids as a possible explanation for the differences. The intestinal barrier helps separate the gut’s contents from surrounding tissue, while bile acids help digest fats. How microbes interact with that barrier and those acids appears to influence whether these processes promote or reduce inflammation.
“The colitis-promoting effects of beef protein were microbially mediated,” the authors say.

Further experiments revealed that beef protein altered the balance of intestinal bacteria and was associated with a thinner protective mucus layer and higher levels of certain bile acids linked to inflammation. In contrast, pea protein supported a different microbial balance and bile acid profile.

The authors also found that adding psyllium, a soluble dietary fiber, to the beef-protein diet reduced inflammation in mice, suggesting that other dietary components may help counteract some of these effects.
Protein choices could become a focus of future dietary guidance aimed at helping people manage IBD and reducing disease risk and severity.

articles.title: Algae-powered soft robot arm uses light to grasp and lift small objects
articles.dek: Tiny underwater algae sway gently in the current. All of a sudden, a light shines on them and they form robotlike arms that start to pick up small rocks and put them in…
paragraphs: Tiny underwater algae sway gently in the current. All of a sudden, a light shines on them and they form robotlike arms that start to pick up small rocks and put them in floating baskets. Sounds like science fiction, but researchers from Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have created a small soft robot arm covered with minuscule algae that can grasp and lift objects. And it's powered by light. This next step in biotechnology has been published in Nature Communications .

The tiny robot arm can perform large, reversible bending movements controlled by light. "Our proof-of-concept actuator is a green and soft strip made of two different hydrogel layers, with microalgae growing on its surface," lead researcher Marie-Eve Aubin-Tam explains.

"It is about 2 cm long and 1 mm thick. When exposed to changing light conditions, the strip can bend back and forth. The shape of the actuator can be easily changed to allow for different movement and function."

The robot's movement can be used for simple tasks such as grasping and manipulating small objects, particularly in underwater environments where soft and gentle handling can be useful. As demonstrations, first author Fan Jiang and fellow researchers used the actuator to hook and lift a rubber ring and to grasp a small metal ball.

Beyond grasping, the robot can also reproduce movements found in nature. Its light-controlled bending could, for example, be incorporated into blinds or agricultural devices that change their shape or orientation in response to light. These demonstrations show how the basic bending motion could be developed into both soft robotic and biomimetic functions.

But scientists are often driven by innate curiosity, Aubin-Tam admits, "We didn't start with a specific application. Our goal has always been to bring the research of living materials to new levels. We wanted to explore what becomes possible when living cells are integrated into functional materials."

The microalgae drive the actuator through their metabolism, which depends on light. During illumination, the algae use light energy and CO₂ to create their cellular "fuel" in the form of sugars through photosynthesis, while they also use nitrogen to build cell components. These processes together increase the pH in the hydrogel.

Jiang says, "Since the two hydrogel layers respond differently to pH changes, they swell to different degrees, causing the strip to bend. When the light is switched off, the cellular fuel is 'burned,' releasing CO₂, which shifts the pH back down. Within 10 seconds, the actuator already starts bending in the opposite direction."

According to Aubin-Tam, their new technology could contribute to soft robotic systems that are more autonomous and environmentally responsive in the longer term. "Microalgae are plantlike organisms that are largely self-sustaining. They use light as their energy source through photosynthesis, which gives the actuator potential for long-term operation with minimal external input. In theory, it wouldn't require a lot of energy to run a system based on this technology."

"It is also just exciting to directly visualize the metabolic activity in microorganisms, to be honest. To see synthetic materials actually translate the algae's biological responses into mechanical motion."

articles.title: India capital steps up air pollution controls ahead of winter
articles.dek: India began annual measures on Thursday to tackle toxic air pollution in New Delhi, a megacity of 30 million people regularly ranked among the world's most polluted capitals.
paragraphs: India began annual measures on Thursday to tackle toxic air pollution in New Delhi, a megacity of 30 million people regularly ranked among the world's most polluted capitals.
Delhi's air quality deteriorates in winter, when cooler air traps pollutants close to the ground.
Major sources include coal-fired power plants, traffic, construction and farm stubble burning in neighboring areas.
The Delhi government on Wednesday announced a ban on open garbage burning and ordered food stalls to stop using coal or firewood.

In previous years, such measures have failed to curb pollution, which peaks from November to January, when levels of cancer-causing PM2. 5 microparticles often hit more than 300 micrograms per cubic meter, 20 times the World Health Organization's recommended daily maximum.
Monitors recorded 233 micrograms per cubic meter early Thursday, about 15 times the limit.
The government's Commission for Air Quality Management has predicted air quality to remain "poor" in the coming days.
A study in The Lancet Planetary Health in 2024 estimated that 3. 8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to pollution that exceeded India's own air quality guidelines.
Last year, pollution levels peaked at 846 micrograms per cubic meter, 56 times the WHO limit.
The U. N. children's agency warns that polluted air puts children at heightened risk of acute respiratory infections.
Further restrictions take effect on Nov. 1, including doubled parking fees and work-from-home arrangements for government office staff, aimed at reducing traffic emissions.
Tighter construction rules will also begin then, followed by a complete ban on construction and demolition from Dec. 10 to Jan. 20.

New Delhi introduced seasonal controls on waste burning, solid fuels, traffic and construction to curb winter air pollution. articles.title: Fires Char New Guinea
articles.dek: New Guinea, the world’s second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions , including seasonally dry…
paragraphs: New Guinea, the world’s second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions , including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño , fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights , closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks.

“Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems,” said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. “It’s a horrible situation.”

According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 19, more than any other year on record at that point in the year. “Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it’s very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997,” said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research.

On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons , the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing , vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades.

Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns —has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region , went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea’s National Weather Service . Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service’s data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures , water shortages , and school disruptions .

In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island.

“We’re seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia,” said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. “Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier.”

Over the past two decades , land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining . According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017.

Sumatra’s fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. “Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets,” said Field. “It’s in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we’re generally seeing the most fire.”
Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November.

articles.title: Forgotten Material From the 1960s Is Hiding Something Unexpected
articles.dek: A long-overlooked material has revealed a hidden atomic pattern that challenges conventional expectations about magnetism.
paragraphs: A long-overlooked material has revealed a hidden atomic pattern that challenges conventional expectations about magnetism.

A uranium compound that has received little scientific attention for decades has been found to contain a previously unknown atomic structure with unusual magnetic properties. The discovery could help researchers identify materials capable of supporting faster, more resilient computer memory.

Scientists discovered a repeating, twisted arrangement of atoms known as a chiral superlattice inside uranium oxytelluride (UOTe). The structure appears to play a central role in how electrons move through the crystal, which exhibits an uncommon combination of two different types of magnetism. The findings were published online October 7 in Nature .

Dr. Mengke Liu, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas, discovered the structure while examining crystals synthesized by Dr. Sheng Ran, an associate professor of physics at Washington University in St. Louis. Liu began studying the material while working as a Harvard Quantum Initiative Postdoctoral Fellow, before joining UT Dallas in 2025. Using transmission electron microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy, she investigated the crystal at atomic resolution.

“I was originally studying this material for an entirely different reason,” Liu said. “When I examined it with high-resolution microscopy, I found a naturally occurring superstructure no one had recognized before.”

The newly identified superlattice consists of a larger, repeating atomic arrangement with a predominantly left-handed or right-handed twist, a property known as chirality. The researchers found that this organization influences electron behavior and is associated with the material’s unusual magnetic characteristics.

The crystal displays characteristics of both ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. In ferromagnetic materials, atomic magnetic moments align to produce an overall magnetization. In antiferromagnetic materials, neighboring magnetic moments point in opposing directions, typically canceling one another so that the material has no net magnetization.
“Finding a single material that combines both of these properties is interesting fundamentally,” Liu said.

A research team at Harvard University, led by Dr. Suyang Xu, the John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Natural Sciences and a corresponding author of the study, was independently investigating the same compound. The teams compared results from complementary experiments and conducted additional measurements, confirming that the unusual atomic superstructure is an important factor controlling how electrons travel through the material.

Antiferromagnetic materials offer potential advantages for computer memory because they are generally less sensitive to external magnetic fields and can support faster operation than conventional ferromagnets. A material combining characteristics of both could provide new possibilities for magnetic memory technologies, although practical devices based on the discovery have not yet been demonstrated.
“If those advantages can be harnessed, memory devices could potentially become both faster and more robust,” Liu said.

Computational analyses also suggest that hundreds of related compounds might contain comparable superlattice structures. This expands the range of materials researchers can investigate for similar electronic and magnetic behavior.

“This study provides a new way of looking for materials with these unusual properties,” Liu said. “Instead of focusing only on the fundamental atomic arrangement, we can also now explore larger superstructures that might influence how electrons behave.”

Uranium oxytelluride was first known to scientists decades before the discovery of its unusual superlattice. Modern microscopy techniques have now made it possible to examine structural features that earlier investigations could not resolve.

articles.title: Study Finds the Arctic Could Lose Far More Sea Ice Than Scientists Previously Predicted
articles.dek: Clues from a warmer Arctic 6,000 years ago suggest the region could lose a million square kilometers more winter sea ice than scientists previously expected.
paragraphs: Clues from a warmer Arctic 6,000 years ago suggest the region could lose a million square kilometers more winter sea ice than scientists previously expected.

The loss of Arctic sea ice has been linked to colder winters and heavier snowfall in the UK, the rest of northern Europe, and North America. The ice regulates how much heat and moisture the ocean releases into the atmosphere, so changes in its cover can influence weather far beyond the polar region.

Climate models disagree most about how much ice will cover the Arctic in winter, making its future particularly difficult to predict. Using evidence from a warmer Arctic 6,000 years ago, researchers have now revised those projections downward by about one million square kilometers, or roughly 386,000 square miles. The findings, published in Nature Geoscience , come after the Arctic recorded its lowest maximum sea ice extent since modern measurements began in March 2025, a record tied again this year.

Researchers from the University of Cambridge and the Centro de Investigación en Matematicas (CIMAT) in Mexico compiled the largest-ever database of a key substance produced by algae living in sea ice. Called IP25, this biomarker was measured in ocean sediment cores dating to the mid-Holocene, when subtle shifts in Earth’s orbit contributed to warmer Arctic conditions and reduced ice cover. Alongside IP25, the team measured complementary biomarkers from organisms that live in open water. Together, these traces allowed them to estimate how much sea ice covered the ocean thousands of years ago.

“The scientific community has amassed lots of paleoclimate records over recent decades, but it’s remained a challenge to directly link these records to future projections, since there is uncertainty at both ends,” said lead author Crystal Fu, from Cambridge’s Scott Polar Research Institute.

By comparing their reconstruction with simulations of the mid-Holocene from 27 climate models, the researchers could assess how closely each model reproduced the ancient ice conditions. They used a statistical method called Bayesian weighting to give greater influence to models that matched the evidence more closely. Those weights could then be applied to simulations of the recent past and future because the same physical processes govern sea ice across different climates.

Although the mid-Holocene warming had a different cause from today’s warming, Fu said the ice would respond in the same way. “It doesn’t matter if the warming is natural variation or caused by human activity: if it warms, sea ice is going to melt,” she said.
In the historical simulations, the weighting removed the models’ collective tendency to overestimate winter sea ice, while the range of uncertainty in the projections narrowed by as much as 85%.

“When we apply the model weights to historical simulations, we completely eliminated the positive bias,” said Fu. “The future projections similarly end up being lower than previous estimates, by about a million square kilometers.”

Applying the revised weights to precipitation projections also suggested that snowfall over southeast Greenland and rainfall in the Mediterranean may be underestimated. The researchers described these as hints that effects beyond sea ice could be larger than expected, with possible implications for the Greenland ice sheet’s stability and future flood risk in southern Europe.

“By using evidence from the past, we can now produce more reliable maps of where Arctic winter sea ice is likely to disappear,” said co-author Marco Aquino-López, of CIMAT. “These give us a much clearer picture of what the Arctic might look like in the coming decades, and how much uncertainty remains.”
The research was supported in part by the US National Science Foundation and the Cambridge Trust. Crystal Fu is a Member of Girton College, Cambridge.

articles.title: Faster to Science: A Letter to the Science Community
articles.dek: NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions.
paragraphs: NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall, from NASA Headquarters, to explain our new Competition Model 2. 0 (CM 2. 0), and answer your questions.

We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long. It has taken years to move mission concepts through the current two-step process. This has often come with contract management challenges, unpredictability, and not enough funding. NASA is committed to doing better — and I’m excited to share with you how we’re making it happen.

I am so pleased that NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has empowered the Science Mission Directorate to take action and make our mission selection process move more smoothly, efficiently, and effectively. The Administrator has directed us to accelerate the delivery of science, reduce the time and resources spent on long competitive processes, and focus funding on the highest-priority missions across every NASA Science division as quickly and affordably as possible. Predictability in delivering incredible science will be at the forefront of what we do.

We are committed to getting this right. Some of these changes will take time to fully implement. We will roll them out in stages, be thoughtful about them, and refine them with your input along the way. But time is also of the essence. By streamlining how missions are proposed, reviewed, and selected, we can make meaningful change right now. That streamlined approach is Competition Model 2. 0, or CM2. 0, and it is how we are answering the Administrator’s call to get you to science faster.

CM2. 0 starts from a simple idea: compete on the science first. Proposals will be science-focused and will not require detailed engineering plans, cost, and implementation work until they are truly needed to make a decision. This frees you to spend more of your time doing science and less of it proposing how to do science.
Here is how we will streamline mission selection across our mission classes:

CM2. 0 will not change how we manage our largest missions since that process has already been reformed. After the James Webb Space Telescope, NASA conducted the Large Mission Study which drew lessons from Webb and best practices from our most successful flagships into a single, documented approach for building large missions more efficiently. Flagships will continue to follow that approach, with NASA directing the overall mission to a lead NASA Center and it will then compete the science teams and instruments through targeted solicitations.
These missions will move to a new, accelerated two-step competition:

These updates in the mission selection process will reduce time from AO to step 2 selection by up to 45 percent. This means that the original 35-months timeline will be reduced to about 19. 5 months, all while having a stronger, more mature mission at the time of selection.

These missions follow the same two-step approach with an even broader field of implementing organizations, including universities and industry partners. Implementing organizations and partners will be evaluated on past performance on projects of similar complexity and cost prior to mission selection. PI-led teams can request pairing with either a Goddard or JPL implementation team at Step 1 selection, and NASA can provide Center support where it will help with procurement, contract management, or quick resolution of technical challenges. This will result again in an up to a 45 percent reduction in the selection timeline.

These missions will move to a single-step competition with a smaller review team and virtual site visits. They will also be open to a broad range of implementing organizations. The time to final selection will drop from about 32 months to about 19 months which is a reduction of up to 40 percent. Our smallest missions will be riding the momentum of a maturing commercial space economy and will move even faster. This means more missions, more often, with more incredible science at a lower cost.

articles.title: A Massive Volcanic Eruption Devastated Japan 7,300 Years Ago – but Survivors Found a Way To Thrive
articles.dek: Survivors of Japan’s ancient volcanic catastrophe may have found a lifeline along the coast, where communities grew even as more distant populations faltered.
paragraphs: Survivors of Japan’s ancient volcanic catastrophe may have found a lifeline along the coast, where communities grew even as more distant populations faltered.

Around 7,300 years ago, the Kikai-Akahoya eruption damaged ecosystems and made parts of Japan uninhabitable for the Jomon people, who lived there by hunting and gathering. Yet some Jomon populations continued to grow through the disaster and its aftermath, while population growth stalled or reversed in more distant areas.

For decades, archaeologists have debated whether the eruption brought an “apocalypse” that abruptly ended all human life closest to its epicenter or whether local populations survived even relatively nearby. A new international study led by Lund University finds that neither total collapse nor simple continuity fully explains what happened.

“This eruption must have been devastating, exploding out of the sea bed with little warning. It battered the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and enormous tsunamis, and then blanketed the landscape with meters of volcanic ash,” explains senior author Peter Jordan, professor of archaeology at Lund University.

The researchers found that populations declined as ecosystems deteriorated and areas became uninhabitable. In southern Kyushu, however, Jomon populations had been shrinking long before the eruption. The disaster struck a region that was already sparsely populated and visited only by highly mobile groups.

Northern Kyushu had a different population history. Its population was growing before the eruption, and that trend continued through the disaster and its aftermath despite extensive, lasting ecosystem damage. The authors suggest that “refugees” moving out of the worst-hit areas immediately after the eruption may have helped sustain that growth.

Survivors from inland areas appear to have moved away and clustered along northern coastlines, where marine ecosystems recovered quickly. New ways of drawing on the sea’s abundant resources may also have accelerated population growth.

“The disaster caused major loss of life. However, survivors migrated, forged new social relations, innovated new kinds of economy, and appear to have found creative ways to exist and later thrive in the new post-disaster conditions,” says lead author Enrico Crema, professor at Cambridge University.

In more distant parts of Japan, populations that had been growing before the eruption stagnated or declined afterward. These far-reaching effects had not previously been identified. They may have been linked to short-term climate change triggered by the eruption or to extreme tooth wear in the deer and boar that Jomon communities relied on for food. The animals may have suffered that dental damage while grazing in ash-covered landscapes. Other volcanic effects on human health and well-being could also have contributed.
For Jordan, the contrasting outcomes demonstrate how complex and unpredictable the aftermath of a major disaster can be.

“This study helps in creating a deeper understanding of the contingent ways in which cultures and societies cope with sudden shocks and catastrophes. Even in the most impossible situations, survivors and communities have choices, however limited: they need to act and make decisions, they need to adjust, collaborate and find new connections and social networks,” he concludes.

articles.title: James Webb Finds a Tiny World’s Rings Changing in Opposite Ways
articles.dek: James Webb has revealed unexpected changes in Chariklo’s two rings, which appear to be evolving in opposite ways over only a few years.
paragraphs: James Webb has revealed unexpected changes in Chariklo’s two rings, which appear to be evolving in opposite ways over only a few years.

For much of modern astronomy, rings were believed to belong only to the giant planets of the Solar System, including Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. That assumption changed in 2013, when astronomers discovered two dense rings around Chariklo, a small body only about 250 kilometers across that travels between Saturn and Uranus at nearly 17 times the Earth-Sun distance.

On October 18, 2022, researchers led by the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia (IAA-CSIC) used the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) to examine Chariklo’s rings during a stellar occultation. This method tracks how a star’s light dims as an object passes in front of it. A new study published in Science Advances, also led by the IAA-CSIC, now shows for the first time that Chariklo’s rings can change measurably over the course of only a few years.

“By comparing JWST observations with those obtained during other stellar occultations over the last decade, we discovered opposite changes in the two rings: while the inner ring shows significantly higher opacity, the outer ring shows lower opacity, ” explains Pablo Santos-Sanz, an IAA-CSIC researcher who leads the study.

The contrasting changes suggest that Chariklo’s rings are not static structures. Instead, the system appears to be active and may be influenced by physical processes that are more complicated than astronomers previously realized.

The observations also marked an important technical milestone. Chariklo’s passage in front of the star was the first stellar occultation that had been specifically predicted and planned for JWST and then successfully observed by the space telescope.

“Achieving this required knowing with extraordinary precision the orbit of Chariklo, the position of the star—thanks to ESA’s Gaia mission—and the trajectory of JWST itself around the L2 Lagrange point, a region of space located about 1. 5 million kilometers beyond Earth, away from the Sun. JWST follows an orbit around this region that requires periodic corrections through station-keeping maneuvers,” notes Yücel Kilic, postdoctoral researcher at the IAA-CSIC and co-author of the study.

During the occultation, Chariklo was moving relative to JWST at only 2. 5 kilometers per second. That unusually slow relative motion gave astronomers exceptional spatial resolution, allowing them to probe the fine structure of the rings in greater detail.

Chariklo’s rings are extremely narrow, and the object itself is so distant that the rings cannot be directly photographed, even by JWST or the largest telescopes on Earth. Stellar occultations provide another way to study them. As Chariklo and its rings pass in front of a background star, each ring produces a brief dip in the star’s brightness, revealing information about the ring’s structure and opacity.

Scientists had generally assumed that rings around small Solar System bodies remain relatively stable over time. The newly detected changes in Chariklo call that assumption into question and suggest that such ring systems may evolve much more quickly than expected.

“Our results force us to rethink how they form, how they evolve, and what mechanisms maintain their stability. The ability to detect these changes opens a new window for understanding the evolution of these systems and, possibly, that of other ring systems in the Solar System,” says Santos-Sanz.

Exactly what caused the changes is still uncertain. They may reflect genuine evolution within the rings over time, differences caused by the filters used during separate observations, or some combination of the two.

articles.title: SpaceX Rocket Creates a Spectacular Glowing “Jellyfish” in the Sky
articles.dek: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a spectacular glowing “jellyfish” in the sky on October 13, 2026, as sunlight lit up its expanding exhaust plumes during an early morning…
paragraphs: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a spectacular glowing “jellyfish” in the sky on October 13, 2026, as sunlight lit up its expanding exhaust plumes during an early morning launch. The unusual display, visible across the eastern United States, formed as the rocket carried SpaceX’s Dragon spacecraft toward the International Space Station.

Known as a “jellyfish,” this striking phenomenon occurs when a rocket launches near sunrise or sunset. Sunlight illuminates the spreading exhaust high above Earth, producing a bright, glowing cloud that resembles the shape of a jellyfish.

The mission lifted off at 6:33 a. m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. It marked SpaceX’s 35th commercial resupply mission for NASA, delivering scientific experiments, essential supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
While the rocket’s illuminated exhaust created a spectacular sight across the eastern United States, its cargo could help support important advances in space technology and medical research.

Among the items aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, or IROSAs. These solar arrays are scheduled for installation later this fall and will help expand the station’s ability to generate electricity.

The spacecraft is also transporting equipment for producing artificial retinas in microgravity, a research effort that could eventually lead to treatments that restore vision on Earth. Another investigation involves 3D heart tissue models, which could help researchers develop methods for conducting drug testing on a larger scale during future space missions.

Additional experiments will explore how a new type of glass forms in the near-weightless conditions of space. Scientists will also study brain organoids, miniature models of brain tissue that could help identify potential treatment targets for neurological diseases, including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis.

articles.title: NASA Conducts RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
articles.dek: NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi.
paragraphs: NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi.
Test teams fired the developmental engine for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket.
During the test, operators also fired the engine up to the 111% power level, matching the thrust needed for new production engines to launch the SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft to orbit.

The main objectives of the test were to acceptance test RS-25 flight components for future Artemis missions and validate the new thermal protection system, which protects the RS-25 engine nozzle from the thermal environment surrounding SLS during launch.

While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability.
Four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket for each Artemis mission.
All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions.

articles.title: NASA JPL Looks to Next 90 Years of Innovation, Exploration
articles.dek: Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars.
paragraphs: Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars.

When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; it’s paving the way for many to come.

Initially a contractor for the U. S. Army, JPL launched America’s first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth.

The lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U. S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7 . It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones.

“Over the course of 90 years, JPL’s first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL’s director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the mission’s most iconic images. “We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and we’re ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.”

Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASA’s Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall , a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the Sun’s activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans.

Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks that other telescopes can’t find. Once an object is spotted, NASA can offer a threat assessment and plan accordingly.

Closer to home, the same lab that launched the first oceanographic satellite in 1978 is at work on several missions that will offer a deeper reading of Earth’s vital signs. Where one mission will monitor the movement of water by measuring slight changes in gravity, another will study how powerful tropical convective storms form. A third will detail how different types of air pollution affect human health.

They add to a fleet of other Earth missions and projects JPL helps lead, including NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) a joint mission with the Indian Space Research Organisation that can pinpoint how Earth’s surface changes in relation to natural disasters. Another, one of a series of instruments called AVIRIS (Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer), can even detect rare Earth elements critical to modern technology.

Flown on airplanes, the AVIRIS sensors were developed at JPL’s Microdevices Laboratory , which invented the “camera on a chip” technology that enables cellphones to take pictures. It’s also where the detectors are being developed for PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), a newly announced NASA mission that will strengthen humanity’s understanding of the universe by studying radiant energy visible only in the far-infrared.

articles.title: NASA to Conduct NCAA Flyover, Engage Fans at University of Alabama
articles.dek: As part of the agency’s Inspiration Tour, NASA will conduct a flyover at the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, Oct.
paragraphs: As part of the agency’s Inspiration Tour, NASA will conduct a flyover at the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, Oct. 24. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will pilot one of three F-5 fighter jets during the flyover, highlighting NASA’s contributions to aeronautics and the agency’s continued commitment to advancing aviation technologies.

Ahead of the game, members of the news media are invited to visit the NASA Experience Zone on Champions Lane, where Isaacman will participate in a media opportunity at 11 a. m. CDT. Media interested in attending should confirm their attendance by 12 p. m. Friday, Oct. 23, with Lance D. Davis at lance. d. davis@nasa. gov to receive additional details and instructions.

Supported by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the NASA Experience Zone will be open to the public from 10:30 a. m. to 2:30 p. m. CDT, with no game ticket required. The experience will give visitors an opportunity to meet NASA team members and learn more about the people and technologies advancing the agency’s missions in aeronautics and space exploration.
Attendees can engage with NASA team members and explore exhibits highlighting the agency’s Artemis campaign and efforts to return astronauts to the Moon, including:

With stops across the nation, NASA’s Inspiration Tour convenes academic, industry, and public sector stakeholders to connect the agency with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space.

The tour will culminate in MAX POWER, a public exposition of American air and space innovation, Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Held in honor of America’s historic 250th anniversary, the multi-day, family-friendly event will showcase the next-generation aircraft, spacecraft, autonomous vehicles, and technologies that will help define the future of transportation in air and space.
